Industry News: Russia’s VTB Opens Bitcoin Trading as Central Bank Finalizes Crypto Test

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian bank VTB began letting brokerage clients buy and sell bitcoin in its investing app on Friday, a day after the Bank of Russia approved the knowledge test every Russian crypto buyer now has to pass.
  • Industry observers note that starting Nov.
  • Industry observers note that “In our model, access to cryptocurrencies will require qualified investor status and passing special testing,” Andrei Yatskov, head of brokerage services at VTB, said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian bank VTB began letting brokerage clients buy and sell bitcoin in its investing app on Friday, a day after the Bank of Russia approved the knowledge test every Russian crypto buyer now has to pass.

Industry observers note that starting Nov. 27, clients of VTB’s brokerage can trade cryptocurrencies in the VTB My Investments app, the broker said. For now, the trades happen over the counter rather than on an exchange, and access is limited to qualified investors, the legal term for Russians who meet wealth or experience thresholds, who also pass the new test.

Industry observers note that “In our model, access to cryptocurrencies will require qualified investor status and passing special testing,” Andrei Yatskov, head of brokerage services at VTB, said. He said the test would appear in the app on Nov. 27 and work like the bank’s existing tests for other instruments.

VTB handles the buying, storage and record-keeping itself on Russian infrastructure. To trade, clients need to open a separate digital account at VTB’s digital depository, where the crypto is held, on top of their regular brokerage account. The bank received its digital depository and crypto exchange licenses on Oct. 6.

“At the start, we will focus on buying and selling cryptocurrencies, and then we will introduce additional services as regulation develops,” Yatskov said.

The launch came swiftly after the regulator moved. On Nov. 26, the Bank of Russia approved the first basic standards for brokers and crypto exchange offices, setting the rules for the test. Every investor has to take it, qualified or not, and it is free.

Buyers must answer at least seven of eight questions correctly. The standard lays out eight topic blocks, from regulation, technical basics and information security to stablecoins, low-liquidity coins, address labeling and blocked transactions, and volatility, with one question drawn at random from each.

Investors who fail can try once more the same day, with different questions. Brokers are barred from sharing the correct answers with clients or telling them which questions they missed. A passing result stays valid for one year from the test date or the latest trade, whichever comes later.

It has been revealed that the test was the missing piece for Russian banks. When retail buying became legal on Nov. 17, T-Bank noted it was waiting on a market standard for testing, and VTB said it was waiting on the remaining rules. Under the broker standard, the industry’s self-regulatory organization has three working days after publication to send brokers the answer options and correct answers.

Ordinary investors still face tight limits once they pass. Non-qualified buyers can only purchase bitcoin, ether and Tether’s USDT, and no more than 300,000 rubles a year through a single intermediary.

In a recent development, exchange trading is next. SPB Exchange noted Friday it will open spot trading in bitcoin, ether and USDT against the ruble on Dec. 1, after the Bank of Russia added it to the registry of digital depositories on Nov. 27. Trading will run from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Moscow time, with same-day settlement in rubles.

Investors won’t all get in on day one. SPB Exchange noted brokers will first use the market to set up their systems, and access will open as each broker is ready. TRX and USDC are also approved, but only for qualified investors, with a start date still to come.

In a recent development, russian exchanges have been allowed to run organized crypto trading since Nov. 22, once the central bank signs off on their rules. Moscow Exchange has also been aiming to open bitcoin trading on Dec. 1.

“We expect that in 2027, as brokers become ready, investor access to the spot market will expand and latest products and investment services will appear,” said Evgeny Serdyukov, SPB Exchange’s chief executive.

Why Sleep Consistency May Be the Missing Piece When It Comes to Heart Health

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, you probably already know that getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night is one of the best things you can do for your health and wellbeing.
  • Sources indicate that as it turns out, your heart might not be too happy about that.
  • According to recent reports, before you start stressing over every late night or weekend sleep-in, though, there's some vital context to understand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you probably already know that getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night is one of the best things you can do for your health and wellbeing. But what happens if you’re consistently hitting that goal while going to bed at different times? Think 10 p.m. on Monday, midnight on Wednesday, and well past 1 a.m. on Saturday because it’s the weekend, after all.

Sources indicate that as it turns out, your heart might not be too happy about that. Newly introduced research suggests that sleep consistency—which includes both when you go to bed and wake up, and how much sleep you get from night to night—could play an vital role in cardiovascular health. And, while getting the recommended amount of shut-eye still matters, researchers are finding that how much your sleep fluctuates may deserve some attention, too.

According to recent reports, before you start stressing over every late night or weekend sleep-in, though, there's some vital context to understand. Here's what the research actually found, why your body seems to care so much about routine, and how consistent your sleep schedule really needs to be.

In a recent development, meet the experts: Nguyen Minh Tuan Viet, MD, PhD, is a neuroscientist and postdoctoral research fellow at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School and lead researcher of the newly introduced study. Nour Makarem, PhD, is a cardiovascular epidemiologist in the department of epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health. Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, is a professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

For the upcoming study published in Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes, researchers analyzed more than one million nights of sleep data from 10,362 adults participating in the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program, an initiative that aims to collect data from over one million Americans and create the country’s largest biomedical database.

According to recent reports, unlike previous studies that only looked at people's sleep habits for about a week, this one used about six months of Fitbit data to see how participants' bedtimes, wake-up times, and total sleep duration changed from night to night. They then compared those patterns with participants’ medical records and tracked their health for nearly four years.

Recent findings suggest that the findings were pretty eye-opening: For every additional 29 minutes of variation in how long someone slept from night to night, their relative risk of serious heart problems, including heart attacks, heart failure, heart muscle disease, and certain strokes, was 24 percent higher. To be clear, that doesn't mean going to bed 29 minutes later than usual on a given night increases your heart disease risk by 24 percent. The researchers were looking at a statistical measure of how much someone's total sleep duration varied over time, rather than the consequences of one late bedtime. As of now, all this information does it point to a potential link between sleep schedule variation and heart disease.

Researchers also found that greater night-to-night fluctuations in bedtime and wake-up times were associated with a 23 percent and 20 percent higher relative risk of cardiovascular problems, respectively. This means that both the consistency of your sleep schedule and the consistency of the duration of that sleep may play a role in heart health.

According to recent reports, there are a few things worth keeping in mind, though. For starters, this study found a connection between inconsistent sleep and heart problems, but it couldn't prove that irregular sleep is what causes those problems. In fact, Viet points out that the relationship could work in the opposite direction too (i.e. early illness might actually make someone’s sleep more irregular). Plus, most participants were women and white, so we can't necessarily assume the findings apply to everyone. Still, the results add to growing evidence that sleep consistency deserves a place in the heart-health conversation.

Your body has its own internal clock, known as your circadian rhythm, which determines when you're tired, when you're wide awake, and even how bodily functions like blood pressure and heart rate change throughout the day. And, it works at its best when it has a reasonably predictable schedule to follow. When you're constantly changing when you sleep and wake, you may disrupt that rhythm, a phenomenon known as circadian misalignment, explains Nour Makarem, PhD, a cardiovascular epidemiologist in the department of epidemiology at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

According to recent reports, that disruption can impact some pretty key cardiovascular processes, like how your body regulates blood pressure. Under normal circumstances, blood pressure usually drops by about 10 to 20 percent while you're sleeping to give your cardiovascular system a period of rest, but research by Makarem suggests that irregular sleep patterns may be associated with higher blood pressure and an increased risk of hypertension. “This is problematic because higher nocturnal blood pressure and having a non-dipping profile (blood pressure that does not dip or dip enough during sleep) are associated with higher risk for heart disease and stroke, the leading causes of death in women,” she claims.

Industry observers note that your sleep schedule may also interact with other daily rhythms, including when you eat and exercise. These behaviors help regulate biological clocks throughout your body, including those involved in metabolism, Makarem indicates. When those clocks fall out of sync, processes like blood sugar regulation may be affected, too. In fact, research has linked irregular sleep patterns with poorer glucose regulation and a higher risk of metabolic concerns.

Research is still emerging, but scientists are noticing some important links between sleep consistency and heart health. A 2025 study published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health followed more than 72,000 adults and found that people with irregular sleep patterns had a higher risk of major cardiovascular events, including heart attacks and strokes. Another study published in Sleep in 2024 analyzed sleep patterns in more than 60,000 adults and found that sleep regularity was a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration in that population.

Industry observers note that so, does this mean having a consistent bed and rising time matters more than getting eight hours? Not necessarily. "The evidence for sleep regularity is rather nascent relative to that for sleep duration," says Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, a professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research at Columbia University Irving Medical Center. She explains that while several studies have made the connection between irregular sleep and poorer health outcomes, more research needs to be done to determine whether making someone's sleep schedule more consistent can actually lower their cardiovascular risk. And, we do have plenty of evidence that getting enough sleep has positive affects on just about every system in the body, from brain function to muscle recovery.

Overall, there are still things researchers are learning about sleep consistency and heart health, but it’s safe to start thinking of it as another piece of the puzzle, alongside getting enough hours and making sure those hours are restorative.

Industry observers note that here's the million-dollar question: Does protecting your heart mean going to bed at exactly 10:30 p.m. every single night, no exceptions? Thankfully, no.

Ultimately, you’ve got some wiggle room. "In general, we would recommend that individuals try not to deviate by 60 min up or down from their average bedtime or sleep duration," states St-Onge, but the smaller the gap, the better.

Think of that as a target, not a hard-and-fast rule. An occasional late night or weekend sleep-in isn’t a reason to panic. What matters more is establishing a reasonably consistent pattern over a period of time rather than expecting yourself to follow a perfect schedule every single night.

Recent findings suggest that if you've had a particularly short night, St-Onge recommends trying to go to bed a little earlier and waking up a little later when your schedule allows, rather than trying to make up for all that lost sleep by sleeping in for hours. Most importantly, don't sweat it. "If one night is off, it's not all doom and gloom; you get right back on schedule the following night," says St-Onge.

Here are a few small changes experts recommend to improve your sleep routine without completely overhauling your lifestyle.

Recent findings suggest that before committing to being in bed every night by 9 p.m., consider what will actually make sense for your schedule. Earlier isn't automatically better. What's crucial is getting adequate sleep on a schedule that works with your body's natural rhythm and everyday responsibilities, explains St-Onge.

Industry observers note that if your current bedtime is midnight but you'd ideally like to be asleep by 11, there's no need to make that change all at once. Makarem recommends gradually shifting your bedtime earlier by about 10 minutes each day until you reach your target. The idea is to give your body time to adjust rather than suddenly expecting yourself to fall asleep an hour earlier than usual.

It's tempting to stay up late on Friday and Saturday nights and make up for it by sleeping well into the morning, but even those brief changes can leave you feeling out of sync by the time Monday rolls around. If possible, St-Onge recommends keeping your weekend bedtimes within about an hour of your usual routine.

If you wear an Apple Watch or Fitbit to bed, you know how easy it is to get caught up in the numbers. One morning you're celebrating a great sleep score, and the next you're wondering what went wrong because your tracker notes you barely got any deep sleep.

While these devices can be helpful for spotting patterns, the last thing you want is to start losing sleep over your sleep. Makarem recommends using trackers to keep tabs on your habits or remind you when it's time for bed, but only if they're actually helping. If checking your sleep stats is making you anxious, it's fine to ditch the data and simply pay attention to when you're going to bed and waking up.

And remember, you don't have to get your sleep schedule exactly right every single night to do something good for your heart. Small changes that you can actually stick with are worth more than chasing a perfect score. As Makarem puts it, "Progress is better than perfect.".

Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension a Month After $6.3 Billion Hack

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it put in place after last month’s record $6.3 billion hack, saying its recovery work is complete and that withdrawals are open across nearly all networks.
  • Sources indicate that “Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted,” the exchange mentioned in an X post Thursday afternoon.
  • According to recent reports, the enhancement closes out a month of phased reopenings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it put in place after last month’s record $6.3 billion hack, saying its recovery work is complete and that withdrawals are open across nearly all networks.

Sources indicate that “Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted,” the exchange mentioned in an X post Thursday afternoon. A small number of networks remain paused for maintenance, which Binance called standard practice and said was unrelated to the hack.

According to recent reports, the enhancement closes out a month of phased reopenings. Binance confirmed the breach on Oct. 29, saying its initial investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave the attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawals.

Sources indicate that the world’s largest crypto exchange stopped all customer withdrawals for two days after the theft, Reuters reported. When they first reopened, customers pulled a net $4.7 billion off the platform, Binance said on Nov. 2.

Binance said on Nov. 12 that it had completed coverage of the affected assets with more than $6.34 billion of firm funds. The money came from a partial draw on its Secure Asset Fund for Users, part of its futures insurance fund and its corporate treasury, and the exchange pledged to rebuild SAFU to about $1 billion.

Coverage is not the same as recovery. Binance replaced the stolen tokens from its own books, while about $2.85 billion of the stolen funds have been frozen remotely by the companies that issue them. The rest remains in the hands of the attackers.

U.S. authorities have blamed North Korean hackers for the theft, which North Korea denies. On Nov. 23, the Justice Department moved to forfeit more than $1.1 billion in USDC that Circle froze, and stated the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion since the attack.

It has been revealed that the unfrozen funds are on the move. North Korean launderers have stepped up transfers through THORChain and a coinjoin service in recent days, blockchain researchers told Reuters, as part of an operation spanning tens of thousands of transactions across blockchains.

It has been revealed that chainalysis and Elliptic estimate that more than $600 million of the stolen crypto has passed through THORChain, though Elliptic said that figure could count funds that went through more than once. TRM Labs estimates THORChain earned as much as $1 million in fees from the swaps.

Separately, $342 million has moved through a coinjoin service mostly coordinated by a pseudonymous figure named Kruw, Elliptic said. A coinjoin combines coins from many users into a single transaction, so their origin is no longer visible on the blockchain. Elliptic has said the launderers will still need other services, such as over-the-counter brokers, to turn the coins into cash.

The FBI on Oct. 31 published wallet addresses used by the attacker and asked crypto service providers, including the network of computers that runs THORChain, to block them. In a video posted Thursday, THORChain co-founder Chad Barraford said 98% of trading on the network was for people’s “own individual financial freedom and liberty.”.

Recent findings suggest that THORChain, which describes itself as decentralized, indicates on its website that it does not “censor” transactions or run Know-Your-Customer checks. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, called the FBI’s move to single out the network’s operators “pretty extraordinary.”.

In a recent development, redbord said the laundering could take months or even years, and that cashing out even a fraction would be a windfall for North Korea. The total stolen from Binance equals about a sixth of the country’s estimated gross domestic product.

“They don’t have to get a lot off in order to make this all worthwhile for them,” Redbord said.

#156051. Tech Report: The world’s biggest oil shock could give EVs and solar a boost

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1094 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The world’s biggest oil shock could give EVs and solar a boost

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home.
  • It has been revealed that the world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran.
  • “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” mentioned IEA executive director Fatih Birol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the longer the Strait of Hormuz crisis drags on, the more incentive countries have to get cars off oil and generate more power at home. That’s one of the major takeaways from the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) new “World Energy Outlook 2026,” which examines how the biggest oil supply shock on record could speed up the shift to EVs and solar.

It has been revealed that the world had a cushion at first when Trump kicked all this off with Iran. Well-stocked oil inventories helped buffer the initial shock, and the IEA coordinated a release of emergency oil reserves. Some Gulf oil took routes around the strait. Atlantic Basin exporters shipped more, and China sharply cut its crude imports. Now more of the burden is falling on consumers, who are paying higher prices and cutting back.

“While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” mentioned IEA executive director Fatih Birol.

The IEA has seen EV sales jump in some countries hit by the crisis, along with increased trade in solar panels and batteries. For countries that import a lot of oil and gas, switching to EVs and heat pumps can help reduce their exposure to the next fuel price spike.

“The impact of Hormuz is only just beginning to become clear,” mentioned energy think tank Ember’s chief analyst Dave Jones. “Hormuz will speed up electrification and renewables, likely faster than many people think. So much of the momentum for electrification at COP31 comes from the desire to have cheaper and more secure energy.”.

Solar leads renewables growth in every scenario the IEA models, and nuclear power is growing strongly, too. Energy efficiency and biofuels could also gain ground. The push to use more homegrown energy could have a very different effect in parts of Asia, where some countries that import oil and gas have plenty of their own coal and could keep burning it for longer.

It has been revealed that the world was already using a lot more electricity before the crisis. Since 2019, electricity demand has grown twice as fast as overall energy demand, outpacing global economic growth. Everything from industrial motors and air conditioners to EVs, heat pumps, and data centers is driving that growth. Electricity comes close to 30% of the energy the world actually uses by 2035 in each of the IEA’s exploratory scenarios.

Before the crisis, around 20 million barrels of oil a day moved through the Strait of Hormuz. If shipping stays risky, new pipelines could route some of those barrels around the strait, while buyers turn to other suppliers or use less oil. In that case, the IEA indicates the amount of oil that needs to pass through Hormuz could drop to 8.5 million barrels a day in 2030 and below 2 million by 2035. The Middle East would still be the world’s largest oil-exporting region.

In a recent development, if the conflict is resolved, oil and gas supply could bounce back. A delayed wave of liquefied natural gas could also help bring prices down even as buyers refill their inventories. Faster electrification could take some of the demand out of both markets.

In a recent development, the world is now using more energy to cool its buildings than to heat them for the first time, the IEA says. By 2035, the global population is expected to grow by 650 million and the economy by a third. Energy needs rise gradually in advanced economies, growth slows in China, and India and Southeast Asia lead faster increases across other emerging and developing economies.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s AI. Under the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario, global data center electricity use doubles to 1,000 terawatt-hours by 2030. That buildout is already running into grid and supply chain constraints, and in some places, local opposition. The IEA also flags risks to critical mineral supplies and threats to energy infrastructure from natural hazards and cyberattacks.

Energy-related CO2 emissions stay around today’s levels under current policies. They start to fall under stated policies and drop further in the IEA’s Additional Response Case, which looks at what could happen if governments respond more strongly to the crisis. Even those deeper cuts fall short of what climate goals require. The current and stated policy scenarios point to 2.5C to 2.9C of warming, and the latest round of national climate pledges highlights little sign that countries are speeding up energy-sector emissions cuts.

The green agenda always come in a second place because people cannot see that far out in the future. Stability of the economy and energy independence are much more important drivers and have immediate impact. Local environment boosts like clean air in cities are also immediate drivers while long term reduced medical bills are not. The oil industry is challenged becuase, unlike previous numerous crises, there is an alternative and the green is the new black.

Industry observers note that there’s a more immediate cost, too. More people gained access to electricity and clean cooking in 2025, but higher fuel prices and shortages threaten to slow that progress. Around 720 million people still live without electricity, and nearly 2 billion cook with polluting fuels or technologies.

Industry News: The Most Comfortable Sneakers for Women, Tested by a Style Writer

📅 29 Sep 2023 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • At this point, I’m pretty sure I qualify as the woman who lived in her shoes.
  • Recent findings suggest that so, I present to you the pairs of comfortable shoes—think walking shoes and cross-training shoes—that actually keep me feeling comfortable and supported without slacking on cuteness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

At this point, I’m pretty sure I qualify as the woman who lived in her shoes. Not in a glamorous Carrie Bradshaw kind of way, but in a professional-sneaker-tester kind of way. I probs have at least 30 pairs crowding my closet and entryways right now, and that’s not even counting the pairs I’ve run into the ground or given away to friends and family (you’re welcome). My top priority is always comfort, and while you might find that a given when it comes to sneakers, I’ve tested my fair share of options that make my feet feel stiff and achy.

Recent findings suggest that so, I present to you the pairs of comfortable shoes—think walking shoes and cross-training shoes—that actually keep me feeling comfortable and supported without slacking on cuteness. From memory foam insoles that mold to your foot's unique shape to running shoes with responsive soles that absorb your stride’s shock, these are the most comfortable sneakers for women, tested by myself and other sneaker enthusiasts at Women’s Health.

Sources indicate that the brand ethos of On is to make people feel like they're running on Clouds. It achieves this thanks to its signature Helion Superfoam midsole, which sets itself apart with a construction that blends rigid, stable sections with flexible foam. This combination of materials provides the perfect balance of cushioning and energy return, giving you a bouncy, lightweight feel when your foot hits the pavement. The result is a soft, natural ground feel, rather than an overly bouncy cushioning experience. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi claims this tech alone is why this shoe is an absolute workhorse when it comes to running (and running fast!). It’s her all-time favorite race shoe—she even ran a half-marathon in it.

Industry observers note that according to Accardi, the shoe feels firm but still has enough flexibility that her running gait isn’t impacted. The toebox has a ton of room for movement, but still holds the foot in place so each step feels responsive and energetic. Even when her legs feel like they’re about to give out, these shoes pick her right back up. On’s innovative speedboard, a flexible plastic plate wedged between the footbed and midsole, snaps back into place for a bouncy effect after your feet hit the ground. This means the shoe requires less energy output with each stride, making running feel easier. Plus, the rebound that comes with the underfoot cushioning gives a spring in your step.

Recent findings suggest that I might not run marathons like Accardi, but I love to wear this shoe for walking and casual jogs. The CloudTec system, which uses air pockets in the midsole (the layer between the insole and the outsole), to create the shoe’s cushiony feel, propels me forward with every step, kind of like walking on a trampoline. And while it’s great for getting your steps in, this shoe has that chunky look that’s super on trend right now. I love pairing it with tailored pants and a boxy T-shirt on top for that upgraded activewear vibe.

One thing to note, though, is the sole wears down fast, which we found to be disappointing, especially given that price tag. Accardi states the Clifton 10 has a better tread thanks to its thicker outsole designed for high-friction.

Read more: On Cloudmonster 3 Review.

Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!). That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it literally feels like walking on pillows.

With the most cushioning of any shoe on this list (and the most cushioning Brooks offers), it’s perfect for those who need extra support. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton notes it has extra plush, foamy cushioning, but even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s incredibly stable thanks to Brooks’ signature Guardrails technology, which is a broad base with two pieces of foam on either side of the heel. It reduces the rolling of the foot both inward and outward, so it cradles your foot in place without messing with your stride. According to Appleton, this combination is great for those with higher arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel an ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options (huge win!).

During testing, I did notice that there was some wear and tear on the shoe pretty early on (it had only been a few months of use). The material on the upper of the shoe wore out pretty promptly. While this knocked it down a few points in my book, its supreme comfort still kept this kick at the very top of my list. Plus, I love how many fun colors the shoe comes in—because running and walking should be fun, right?!

Read More: Brooks Ghost Max 3 Review.

The Hoka Clifton 11 is a standout favorite among WH editors. After testing nearly every Hoka model, I can attest that the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar—just a smidge lighter and more springy. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning.

Recent findings suggest that the first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly narrower, too, but it doesn’t feel tight or uncomfortable. I prefer the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

In a recent development, despite its lighter weight, it has a generous stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

I also find that the foam absorbs impact well. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never feel fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride feels smooth and natural whether I’m walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

According to recent reports, so far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the upcoming Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review.

There’s nothing worse than slipping into an uncomfortable shoe after a tough run—that’s where the Alo Recovery Sneaker comes in. Designed to support tired feet, it features a structured sole and high-rebound foam insole that offers arch support and bounces back into place with each step. It makes every step feel stable, cushioned, and balanced. The second I put this pair on after a long run, my feet are instantly relaxed. I can’t say that about most of my other sneakers.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest perks of this shoe? The traction is next-level, which is key for a recovery sneaker that’s meant to keep you comfortable and steady all day. Inside, the sock-like lining prevents your foot from sliding around. The thick ankle collar also helps stabilize the foot and provides extra support up the leg, keeping everything locked in place.

Sources indicate that style-wise, this sneaker goes with everything—sweats, shorts, jeans, leggings, you name it. That’s why I crowned it the best overall platform sneaker. After giving it a spin for a few weeks running around Manhattan, walking my dog around Long Island, and wearing it to and from workout classes, it's done the best job at keeping my feet pain-free compared to many other platform sneakers I've worn. The 1.5-inch platform is subtle but adds just the right amount of height to elongate my legs without being so tall that I feel unstable. Oh, and it’s super cute to boot. I’m a substantial fan of the Natural White colorway, which looks clean and classic, and pairs effortlessly with everything from sweatpants to denim.

Even if you’re not fresh off a run, it works for the office, errands, or a casual lunch. It’s hands down one of the most versatile (and most worn) shoes in my closet. My one con is that it feels a bit heavy and bulky, especially after a long day of wear.

Read more: Alo Recovery Mode Sneaker Review.

Sources indicate that I hadn't tried Asics until this year, and now it's my go-to shoe brand. Not only does its shoe have a streetwear vibe (I'm loving the bright yellow color with sweats and jeans), but they’re also some of the most comfortable shoes I’ve ever worn. In the UB9-S Gel Kayano 20s, the brand uses its signature gel cushioning technology, which features gel units placed in both the heel and forefoot of the shoe to absorb shock and provide a soft landing. This cushioning adapts to your foot’s movement, offering flexibility while reducing impact on your joints. Plus, the form-fitting upper keeps your foot locked in place, making it perfect for long runs, but stylish enough for everyday wear.

I wear this shoe everywhere—on runs, in the gym, and even to the office—and I get compliments virtually every single time I step out in it. The support is unmatched, the traction is solid, and it’s lightweight enough that I never feel weighed down. Plus, it breaks in fast (I wore it right out of the box), so there’s no awkward adjustment period. If you’re looking for a sneaker that can do it all while still looking cool, this is the one for you.

One con to note: It comes in some funky colors, so if you’re not into something bright and fun, I’d recommend looking elsewhere. I also wish it came in a wider version for those with wider feet and bunions.

Read More: Asics Gel-Kayano 20 Review.

Sources indicate that we’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” indicates WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

It has been revealed that now with a lighter weight and a lower heel-to-toe drop (6 mm compared to 9.5 mm), the shoe doesn’t weigh me down and puts less stress on the ankles and feet. I’m a substantial fan of the wider base for lifting and squatting because it makes my feet feel locked. The forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter add extra security, while the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

And post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. I recently wore this sneaker while traveling, and it kept my feet happy power walking through the airport and standing in long security and customs lines. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”.

The fit is true to size, and while wide-size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, the wide outsole may feel too bulky during stair climbing or quick, dynamic moves.

Read More: lululemon Chargefeel 3 Review.

Let me introduce you to my new favorite low-profile, fashion sneaker: the Puma Speedcat. It’s been making waves with style girls, and after testing it out for months, I can see why. This shoe pairs so well with any outfit, with a slim, almost ballet-flat silhouette that doesn’t clash with nicer pieces in my wardrobe. I even see celebs like Em Rata sport the Speedcat all the time, and they always make any streetwear ‘fit look so chic and cool.

In a recent development, like the Samba, it has a pretty flat sole, but I actually find it more cushioned thanks to its EVA midsole, which has a lightweight, cushioned feel and shock-absorbing properties. This means I can walk around for longer without my feet aching. Plus, after wearing it on wet city streets, I’ve noticed it has better traction, which is a huge win.

Recent findings suggest that the only downside? The fit is a little narrow, especially in the toe area. If you have wider feet, I’d definitely recommend sizing up.

Read More: Puma Speedcat OG Review.

Industry observers note that originally designed for indoor soccer, the Adidas Samba has become a cult-favorite sneaker that’s just as popular on the streets as it is on the field. At first glance, the Samba looks pretty flat, so I wasn’t expecting much in terms of comfort. But after logging hundreds of miles walking around the city, I was surprised by how well it supports my feet. The Samba uses a combination of synthetic leather for the upper and a rubber sole with a cushioned midsole for comfort. The cushioning is more subtle compared to high-performance running shoes, but it still provides a soft, supportive feel. Even without a ton of cushioning, I rarely experience discomfort, which is impressive for a sneaker this sleek. It runs narrow, especially for wide feet, and I recommend going a half size down, as it tends to run substantial—many with wider feet or bunions agree it’s not the best fit.

It’s a go-to for effortlessly cool outfits—you can wear it with jeans, dresses, slacks, or shorts and always look stylish. I own this shoe in two different colorways (it comes in so many different shades), and after wearing it with practically everything in my closet, I can confidently say it adds a sporty, trendy touch to any outfit.

One of Under Armour’s first-ever shoes, this kick is rooted in sport. But it’s gotten some essential upgrades since its launch, and it’s safe to say I’m hooked. Since 2009, it’s been updated with leather upper overlays to keep the foot supported and soft UA HOVR cushioning, made from soft EVA foam and rubber, which is engineered to store and release energy with each step, providing a bouncy, responsive feel that helps propel you forward. Out of all the shoes I’ve tried, this pair feels the most bouncy, which I know is an absolute essential for the runners and walkers out there that like that super thick underfoot feel. It also has a rocker shape to keep the foot in a forward motion for less energy exertion.

Sources indicate that the UA Apparition also has a mesh upper for supreme breathability—I’ve worn it during HIIT workouts, runs, and walks and never feel like my feet are constricted or sweaty, but I still feel supported and balanced. With a sleek, minimalistic look, the Apparition pairs well with anything from gym gear to casual streetwear. The rubber outsole provides traction and durability, allowing for smooth transitions during both dynamic workouts and everyday use.

My one con? There are some fun colors available, but I wish there were more options to choose from.

Industry observers note that when it comes to comfortable sneakers, cushioning should be your top priority—whether you’re walking, running, hitting the gym, or just running errands. Here are the cushioning levels you can expect to see in the shoes below:.

Recent findings suggest that as Women’s Health editors, we practically live in sneakers, so we know what it takes for a shoe to feel super comfortable. When I originally put together this list of the most comfortable sneakers in 2025, I spent over two years testing more than 50 pairs in every possible scenario—long and short walks, runs, HIIT workouts, full days out in NYC, travel days, and more. For this 2026 patch, myself and other WH editors re-tested newer iterations of our favorite pairs to make sure they still meet our standards. I also sought advice from fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, as well as style contributor Lily Wohlner. We looked at everything from cushioning and stability to sizing, traction, and color options. And if a pair left our feet aching or uncomfortable, it didn’t make the cut. So you can trust that every sneaker on this list kept our feet happy all day long—even through our toughest workouts.

30 Cool Gifts for Dads That Every Father Will Appreciate

  • According to recent reports, what makes a cool gift for dad these days?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FINDING A GIFT for dad can be a daunting task in the countdown to the holidays. If you have siblings, you especially know what we mean—there's an unspoken competition to see who can impress dad the most.

According to recent reports, what makes a cool gift for dad these days? Well, on top of balancing a fine line between trendy and functional, new and nostalgic, the gifts we've curated are sure to answer a certain calling or scratch an itch he's had for some time. We've gathered an array of remarkable gifts for men, from adjustable (and affordable) kettlebells to a scoreboard ticker to a cozy bathrobe.

Industry observers note that this list is dynamic because that's exactly what fathers are. And it's varied too, also just like all those old men out there. We've got running shoes for jogging dads, gadgets for DIY dads, literature for bookworm dads, and excellent food for hungry dads. He's sure to unwrap something that he will spend a lot of quality time with, right out of the gate.

It has been revealed that they don’t have to be a renowned angler to appreciate a good fishing shirt: They’re stretchy, quick drying, and moisture wicking. Huckberry made this elevated version that can go from the boat to the bar using a lightweight nylon fabric. The double pockets and western yoke are subtle nods to heritage workwear.

In a recent development, this handwoven hammock chair beats his favorite lawn chair by a mile. The acrylic yarn won’t fade, mold, or rot, and the colors stay vibrant without fading. More than a chair, there’s plenty of room to sprawl out for a midday nap or to catch up on a book. Spring for the stand, and they can take this chair anywhere.

Every childhood memory I have of my dad coming home from work includes a pen—he had at least two in the chest pocket of his button-up shirt—and he still keeps one strapped to his wrist today. A reliable pen may seem novel in an increasingly digital world, but that’s what makes it (even more) gift-worthy. The Lamy 2000 has a satisfying click, good looks, and a smooth ballpoint for all his notes and scribbles.

According to recent reports, the Pacebreakers are an excellent do-everything pair of shorts: he can work out, chill out, even swim in them if he’s in a pinch. They come in a bunch of different colors and are available in 5-, 7-, and 9-inch inseams. Hard to find a better pair of active shorts out there.

It has been revealed that A reliable pocket knife comes in handy more often than you think. While he may have his go-to, the Benchmade Bugout is sure to impress with its attention to detail and American-made craftsmanship. The Grivory handle is lightweight and grippy, and the drop point blade has excellent edge retention. It’s a slick addition to the old man’s EDC.

It has been revealed that “Give them something they’ll actually use”—a good starting point when thinking of what to gift a picky dad. Now think about how many times he uses the bathroom. You see where we’re going with this? The Tushy Wave is the brand's most elevated non-electric attachment, and it’ll keep the old man fresh. It’s a snap to set up, easy to use, and will save him money on toilet paper.

It has been revealed that the garage is a sacred place for dads where they can have everything, particularly in or out of place, as they want. These Payloader boxes from Decked will have his tools, gear, and seasonal needs all organized and protected. They’re extremely durable, feature a snap-lock lid, and are made in the U.S.A.

According to recent reports, what dad doesn’t love a significant screen? The MoGo 4 projector delivers a crisp 1080p display so he can project movies, matches, and shows anywhere he pleases. Auto-adjust features make it easy to use, and onboard Google TV, Netflix, and YouTube makes streaming seamless. The projector itself is about the size of a coffee tumbler for easy storage, and onboard speakers mean he doesn’t have to hassle with an external set.

Patagonia’s Black Hole bags are widely popular for good reason—they’re durable, weather-resistant, and look cool. The nylon fabric resists tears and abrasions, and the multiple pockets hold everything he may need. It can double as a large gym bag as easily as it can take him on a weekend getaway. The Black Hole duffle comes in various sizes and colors to suit exactly what he wants.

Industry observers note that for the dad who loves making drinks at home and wants to impress his friends, this cult-favorite book from Death & Co. is packed with more than 500 cocktail recipes, bartending tips, and insider tricks from one of NYC’s most famous bars. His home bar setup will instantly feel a whole lot cooler.

Many speakers can go outside, but Turtlebox is built for it. The Ranger is a fully waterproof speaker that is loud enough to fill the entire backyard. It doesn’t just turn up to the loudest possible decibel, though; it actually sounds good with a deep base and no tinny noises on the high end.

Nothing beats lazing around in a plushy bathrobe, but the summer months call for something a little more breezy. Brooklinen took its ultra-popular bathrobe and shortened it to let some air in on those legs. Even if he already has a bathrobe, consider this his summer style.

DIY projects are not just a game of inches; they can come down to millimeters and more. Give dad some exactness with this great laser measure. It looks ultra-modern and will make his crafty work all the more, according to strategy. It has a range of more than 90 feet and connects right to an app for real-time figures.

It has been revealed that if Dad's always on his phone checking scores, there's a better way. Gift him this cool LED ticker, featuring a pixelated scoreboard built around his top squads. It's like a Lite-Brite set for the sports enthusiast. We've found it's great beyond just tailgating season, too, as you can get news blurbs and weather info, among other things.

We love a good adjustable gym tool. This kettlebell can evolve with his workouts, spanning a weight range of 32 pounds and effectively replacing six individual weights. There's even an associated app with workouts if dad needs a nudge of inspiration to really get going.

Honestly, we were a bit skeptical of this muscle and nerve stimulator. Until we tried it out, and fell for the multiple settings and massage-like treatments that can target very specific areas. There's a precision to the Halo, and it makes recovery all the more enjoyable, not to mention rejuvenating.

Dad taught you all those things; why not return the favor? Go with the wisdom of a real pro, whether it's a culinary figure, an actor, a scientist, or some other notable person. He'll love being a student again. And the number of teachers just keeps growing, in both numbers and professions.

In a recent development, if he's going to cook that meat, set him up with a proper thermometer. Digital is the way to go, as it's more accurate and much easier to deal with. Plus, that'll make less risk of undercooking anything. Even dad can use an assist on the grill from time-to-time. This one won us over by freeing up valuable time as the app will essentially babysit you cooking proteins for you.

Read More: Best Kitchen Gadgets.

Sources indicate that let us generalize a bit here. Dads like fires and they also like DIY. Well, this might be the perfect scratch for those itches, a pizza maker from Solo Stove. He can make his own pies and experience the reward of baking them in a fire-filled pizza oven. Win-win, people. So far here at MH we haven't met a Solo Stove product we didn't like, and this pizza oven is no different.

It has been revealed that here's a novel gift, ideal for the bird fanatic or casual ogler alike. The camera syncs up with your computer or phone and offers HD images of video of your feathered friends. There's even a sensor to let you know when something special might be having a snack.

Porsche’s newest electric car is a tiny 50 mph replica of a legendary racer

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that porsche’s latest electric vehicle isn’t a newly introduced Taycan or Macan EV.
  • Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.
  • It has been revealed that if Hedley Studios sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the firm before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that porsche’s latest electric vehicle isn’t a newly introduced Taycan or Macan EV. In fact, it’s not even a full-sized car. Instead, the German automaker has teamed up with British luxury miniature car builder Hedley Studios to create an 80%-scale electric replica of one of Porsche’s most iconic racing cars, the legendary 550 Spyder.

Known as the Porsche 550 J, the pint-sized electric sports car will make its public debut at the Icons of Porsche festival in Dubai on November 21-22, celebrating 75 years of Porsche motorsport.

It has been revealed that if Hedley Studios sounds familiar, that’s because we’ve covered the firm before, back when it was known as The Little Car Company. Among its more entertaining projects was a life-sized recreation of the famous Japanese Tamiya Wild One RC dune buggy, turning a childhood remote-controlled favorite into an actual drivable electric vehicle. We’ve also covered the company’s ultra-luxurious miniature electric cars, including its stunning Bentley Blower recreation.

Now the firm has turned its attention to Porsche, and the result is perhaps its most impressive miniature EV yet.

There’s something I love about miniature electric cars, combining the fun of four-wheels with the right-sized (or pint-sized) magic of mini-mobility.

The Porsche 550 J is based on the original 550 Spyder, Porsche’s first purpose-built racing sports car, which debuted in 1953 and went on to become a motorsport legend.

Sources indicate that despite being scaled down to 80% of the original’s dimensions, the new electric version still seats two adults. It weighs just 350 kg (772 lb), thanks partly to its lightweight tubular steel spaceframe and hand-formed carbon fiber bodywork.

The standard version features an 8 kW (11 hp) electric motor operating on a 48V system, providing a top speed of 40 mph (65 km/h) and a range of up to 30 miles (50 km).

Recent findings suggest that for those who want a bit more performance from their miniature Porsche, an optional RS Pack doubles the power to 16 kW (21 hp), increases the top speed to 50 mph (80 km/h), and extends the range to 50 miles (80 km) thanks to additional batteries. The upgrade also includes drilled disc brakes and adjustable suspension.

The attention to detail goes well beyond the exterior. The car features Brembo brakes, Bilstein suspension, Continental tires, and even a wood-rimmed Nardi steering wheel, just like the original. The classic dashboard retains its three-dial layout, though the fuel gauge has been replaced with a battery meter and the original choke lever now serves as a drive mode selector.

Even the charging port is cleverly hidden beneath the chrome fuel filler cap.

The project was developed in close collaboration with Porsche over six years, with Hedley Studios gaining access to original engineering drawings, archival materials, and historic vehicles in Porsche’s museum.

Only 250 examples will be produced, with buyers able to choose historic racing liveries or custom paint finishes, including colors matching their full-sized Porsches.

Recent findings suggest that of course, this level of craftsmanship doesn’t come cheap. Prices start at £69,500 (approximately US $91,000), before taxes and options. Orders are already open through Porsche dealers and Hedley Studios, with deliveries expected to begin in spring 2027.

That’s a lot of money for a car that’s only 80% there, but then again, this isn’t really meant to be practical transportation. It’s a collector’s piece that just happens to be electric, drivable, and capable of hitting 50 mph. When there are only 250 of these being built, the £70k price is really just the entry ticket to a special, ultra-luxury club of electric mini-Porsches.

Sources indicate that and if you ask me, that sounds like a pretty fun combination. I don’t think I’ll ever be in the market for one of these personally, but I’d sure love to be friends with someone who is!

In a recent development, bitcoin and most major cryptocurrencies edged slightly higher Thursday as U.S. stock exchanges closed for Thanksgiving, a day after inflation data and fresh tariff concerns rattled markets.

Sources indicate that bitcoin traded at around $60,560 as of just after 1:00 p.m. ET, up 1.39% over the past 24 hours but down 3.67% over the past week, according to Decrypt's price tracker. The largest cryptocurrency has recovered roughly 5% from Wednesday’s low of $57,500.

Ethereum gained 0.87% to just under $1,700, while XRP and Solana rose 3.1% and 2.17%, respectively.

The Nasdaq Composite recovered from an intraday plunge of as much as 4.6% Wednesday to close down 0.62%. The S&P 500 contract for difference (CFD), a derivative tracking the index, was up 0.67% on Thursday at around 7,226 points, per TradingView. The cash index itself was not trading.

Wednesday’s selloff followed a combination of stronger-than-expected U.S. economic growth, proposed tariffs and renewed concerns over AI stocks, as Decrypt previously reported. The Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation, the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, rose 3.8% year over year in October, complicating efforts to bring inflation back to its 2% target.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

According to recent reports, bitcoin’s daily chart looks considerably weaker than its stock market counterpart. Its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA) has crossed below its 200-day EMA, forming a bearish signal known as a death cross. EMAs track average prices over a given period, assigning more weight to recent trading activity.

Both averages are trending lower, with Bitcoin trading roughly 16% below its 50-day EMA of $71,478 and 19% below its 200-day EMA of $74,516, according to TradingView charts.

Industry observers note that the S&P 500 CFD, by contrast, remains in golden cross territory, with its 50-day EMA of 7,517 still above its 200-day EMA of 7,372. The price is below both indicators, however, and the gap between them is narrowing, suggesting the longer-term bullish trend is weakening.

It has been revealed that neither crossover guarantees where prices will go next, but the comparison indicates how much more technical damage Bitcoin has sustained. Bitcoin faces potential resistance between $62,000 and $64,000, while recent lows around $57,500 to $58,500 form a possible support zone, followed by November’s low near $55,000.

Around $7 billion worth of Bitcoin options are due to expire Friday on Deribit, with traders favoring contracts that provide protection against price declines more heavily than they did in October. U.S. stock trading will resume Friday, but the NYSE will close early at 1 p.m. ET.

Elon Musk announces another Tesla vehicle no one asked for

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk notes Tesla plans to build a version of the Model Y with no steering wheel and no pedals, a driverless people-mover he describes as “good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people.”.
  • It’s yet another vehicle nobody asked for, from a firm that ended Model S and Model X production this year and is about to end the Cybertruck.
  • Musk made the comments on stage at the Newly introduced York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk notes Tesla plans to build a version of the Model Y with no steering wheel and no pedals, a driverless people-mover he describes as “good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people.”.

It’s yet another vehicle nobody asked for, from a firm that ended Model S and Model X production this year and is about to end the Cybertruck. And the data claims very few car buyers want a car they can’t drive.

Musk made the comments on stage at the Newly introduced York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

He pitched it as the answer to the Cybercab only carrying two people. “We still need autonomous vehicles if you’ve got 4 or 6, or a whole family,” Musk said, before adding that Tesla plans “an autonomous version of the Model Y that won’t have steering wheels or pedals.”.

There was no timeline, no price and no word on where it would be built.

Six or seven seats points straight at the Model Y L, the stretched three-row Model Y that Tesla launched in the US in July for $61,990, or the regular Model Y with the $2,500 seven-seat option Tesla brought back in January.

According to recent reports, here’s the funny part. When Tesla rolled out the Model Y L in China in August 2025, Musk remarked it might never come to the US, “given the advent of self-driving in America.”.

The idea was that autonomy would make a bigger family car pointless. Less than a year later, Tesla was building the Model Y L at Giga Texas and selling it at the top of the Model Y lineup.

Now Musk wants a driverless version of that same car. So families still need a major vehicle, self-driving or not. That’s what we stated in 2025.

In a recent development, the robotaxi argument doesn’t hold up either. Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet is mostly Model Ys, and those cars have a steering wheel and pedals.

It has been revealed that the wheel isn’t what’s stopping them from driving themselves. Removing it mostly makes the car useless outside Tesla’s geofences.

Industry observers note that we’ve already seen what that looks like. Tesla opened personal Cybercab orders last week at $29,990, but the car only works inside Robotaxi service areas and requires a $299 per month subscription to operate at all.

There’s also the regulatory mess. Tesla self-certified the Cybercab as compliant with federal safety standards even though FMVSS 135 calls for a foot-operated service brake, and NHTSA responded with a Special Order in September. Zoox took the slower route and got a Part 555 exemption, which caps it at 2,500 vehicles a year. A second vehicle with no controls means a second round of that fight.

In a recent development, cox Automotive’s 2026 Autonomous Vehicle Study asked US consumers which level of autonomy they’d find most appealing in a vehicle they own. Only 10% picked fully driverless Level 5, down from 17% when Cox first asked in 2016.

The most popular choice was Level 4 at 28%: full autonomy, but with the option for a human to drive. And only 38% said they’d feel safe in a Level 5 vehicle, compared to 87% for a modern car with basic driver aids.

So after a decade of exposure to self-driving tech, interest in a car with no controls went down, not up.

Tesla already makes the Model Y. It already makes a six-seat Model Y. Just make the Model Y.

According to recent reports, in 2016, Musk’s Master Initiative Part Deux promised to “expand the electric vehicle product line to address all major segments.” Ten years later, once the Cybertruck ends next summer, Tesla’s consumer lineup is the Model 3 and Model Y. That’s it. No affordable car (Musk called a non-robotaxi $25,000 Tesla “pointless” in 2024), no compact crossover, no minivan, no midsize pickup.

Teslafsdtracker is the only real source of Tesla ADS/ADAS capability.

It shows a safety critical intervention is needed every 2000 miles. That is less than 1% of whats needed to remove a human from the real time loop. Hence Tesla's hiding of intervention data and operational parameters, and the control centers where humans watch real time video feeds and initiate interventions when needed.

Tesla L4 is all smoke and mirrors. All they have is a L2 system driving in geo restricted zones with driver oversight shifted from the front seat to a control center.

Every time there’s a gap in Tesla’s lineup, Musk gives the same answer: autonomy will fill it. The Model Y L was going to be unnecessary. The cheap car was pointless. The Model S and X made way for Optimus, and the Cybertruck for the Cybercab.

But Tesla’s own robotaxi fleet proves you don’t need to remove the steering wheel to run a robotaxi. Keeping it costs Tesla almost nothing and keeps the car useful for the roughly 90% of buyers who still want the option to drive. Taking it out only adds a federal compliance fight and shrinks the market to people who live inside a geofence.

Recent findings suggest that if Tesla wants to sell more cars, it should build cars people are asking for. Who exactly is asking for this one?

Pottery Barn Jake Leather Sofa Review, Tested by AD (2026)

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1268 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve wanted a leather sofa for many years, but I could never find a color I liked—a detail just as notable to me as the material.
  • Industry observers note that if you don’t love the stately green hue as much as I do, that hardly means the Jake isn’t your room’s match.
  • The cost of the Jake depends on the size, material, and cushion configuration you choose, falling somewhere between $2,000 and $6,000 for most designs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I’ve wanted a leather sofa for many years, but I could never find a color I liked—a detail just as notable to me as the material. I wasn’t interested in the usual black, brown, or cognac options, instead preferring something less traditional but not squarely trendy. And then I discovered Pottery Barn’s Jake Leather Sofa in Vintage Hunter, which hit my sofa sweet spot, exuding a deep confidence that reads as rich, grounded, and classy. Its sophisticated presence anchors my living room without overpowering the space.

Industry observers note that if you don’t love the stately green hue as much as I do, that hardly means the Jake isn’t your room’s match. The sofa’s customization options—another major selling point—are robust: In addition to being able to choose from a broad range of leathers and upholstery colors, I could also select the style of the seat and back cushions, adding up to a piece of furniture that feels more personal than an off-the-sales-floor purchase. With its slim arms, low profile, plush cushions, and bronze-finished metal legs, it strikes a balance between streamlined and inviting.

How much does it cost? Are there payment looks available?

The cost of the Jake depends on the size, material, and cushion configuration you choose, falling somewhere between $2,000 and $6,000 for most designs. To save yourself from shopping-cart sticker shock, price out the exact model you want, since the leather grade and sofa width can meaningfully change the total. For instance, my 86-inch-wide, 36-inch-deep model in Vintage Hunter retails for $3,999, but a 70-inch-wide, 36-inch-deep loveseat in a Chocolate Performance fabric costs $3,099, and is sometimes on sale for less.

Sources indicate that what are the upholstery or customization options? Did you choose any?

Recent findings suggest that there’s little you can’t choose with the Jake. Available in an extensive selection of leather colors and finishes, you can also pick the number of back cushions you’d like (two or three) and style of seat cushion (two separate or a single bench). For my vintage leather sofa in Hunter, I decided on one bench-style seat cushion and three back cushions.

What is the lead time for customization, manufacturing, and delivery?

It took about six weeks for my sofa to arrive at my home after I ordered it, which felt reasonable for a piece with customized upholstery and cushion selections.

What kind of couch or seating arrangement did you have before, and what drew you to your upcoming couch?

My previous sofa was a smaller turquoise felt sleeper from Mopio that I bought on Amazon; its blue undertones made it feel brighter and more casual. I loved the feel, but dog hair got caught in it easily and was hard to vacuum. This Hunter shade is deeper, moodier, and much closer to the sophisticated design I had envisioned for the room.

What was the delivery process like? What was the assembly process like? How long did it take, and how many people did it require?

Sources indicate that receiving the sofa could not have been easier, thanks to Pottery Barn’s included white-glove delivery service. Two people brought the sofa into my home, placed it where I wanted it, and assembled it on the spot. The entire process took about 10 minutes. For a substantial piece of furniture like this sofa, the luxury delivery experience was a major advantage.

Sources indicate that what are the dimensions? How does it fit in your space? Would it be better suited for a certain type of home?

Industry observers note that I chose the 85-inch-wide version, which measures 36 inches deep and 32 inches high, and it fits my apartment almost perfectly. It feels generous enough to function as the room’s main seating option without commandeering the full focus of the room. I would recommend this size for a midsize living area, provided that the access points can accommodate its width. As always, measuring the doorway, elevator, stairwell, and turning radius before you click “buy” is just as crucial as measuring the piece’s final spot.

Sit test: Is it comfortable? Does it feel well-made? Does the couch have a tendency to sag?

Sources indicate that comfort is where the Jake has exceeded my expectations. It feels supportive and substantial, and the cushions have held their shape without developing an obvious sag. In the four to five months I’ve had the Jake, several visitors have already stayed over and shared that they’ve experienced restful nights on this couch.

The only recurring quirk I’ve experienced is that the seat cushion occasionally slides forward a smidge. It is easy to nudge back into place and has never become a serious annoyance. It’s also entirely possible that this funky detail has more to do with my sitting tendencies than the sofa’s construction.

Is the sofa suitable for particular decor styles and if so, which?

The Jake naturally fits with modern and contemporary interiors. Its low, linear profile, narrow arms, and metal legs provide a clean architectural quality, while the Hunter leather adds depth and character. However, with the right design elements in place, the sofa would also look at home in decidedly relaxed spaces, with warm woods, woven textiles, vintage pieces, or more traditional accessories.

Is it durable and practical in a modern home?

Despite its sophisticated appearance, this sofa isn’t your grandfather’s precious showpiece that exists for looking at and not sitting on. Rather, I’ve found it to be durable, practical, and comfortable to actually use daily.

Recent findings suggest that but that’s just for humans; pets are the bigger consideration here. I have a dog, and a few scratches have already appeared on the leather. My current remediation system is to cover the sofa with a sheet when we are home and remove it before guests arrive. It works, but anyone hoping for completely carefree pet ownership should be realistic about the care needs of a leather sofa before purchasing this polished piece.

The Jake might fare better with children than with a dog, since typical spills are often easy to address rapidly, while claw marks are harder to reverse (if possible to do at all). I am planning to try a leather conditioner to soften the appearance of the scratches, though I have not tested it yet. Before applying any product, I would follow Pottery Barn’s care instructions to spot-test it in an inconspicuous area first. Ultimately, the Jake is probably better suited to a pet-free home, or to any owner willing to go whatever lengths necessary to protect and maintain the leather.

Do the photos do this product justice? Was there anything you were surprised to see IRL?

The sofa looks remarkably similar in person to how it appears online, including the depth of the Hunter color and the overall proportions. There was no unpleasant reveal on delivery day; the sofa I had spent weeks picturing was essentially the sofa that arrived.

Would the couch be easy to move into another room? Would it be easy to move to another apartment or home by yourself?

While it’s more manageable to move than other full-size leather sofas may be, largely in light of its removable legs and loose cushions, I wouldn’t call the Jake a portable sofa. It’s not modular, but rather comes in a single piece, so moving it to another room or home is certainly not a single-person job. However, assuming the doorways and corners cooperate, rehoming its 85-inch span should be possible, so long as you have help on hand.

Comfort: A+Value: ADelivery and assembly: A+Style: A+Overall couch rating: A.
